title: Vector Algebra — Types, Addition and Scalar Multiplication
topicTitle: Scalar and vector quantities, types of vectors; addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors
notes: **Scalar vs vector:** scalars have magnitude only (mass, temperature); vectors have magnitude and direction (displacement, force).

**Types of vectors:** equal vectors (same magnitude and direction), opposite vectors (same magnitude, opposite direction), unit vector (magnitude 1), null vector (magnitude 0), parallel vectors, collinear vectors, coplanar vectors.
**Addition:** $\vec{a} + \vec{b} = \vec{b} + \vec{a}$ (commutative). Triangle law: place tail of $\vec{b}$ at head of $\vec{a}$; resultant closes the triangle.

**Subtraction:** $\vec{a} - \vec{b} = \vec{a} + (-\vec{b})$. Geometrically, draw $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ from same point; $\vec{a} - \vec{b}$ is the vector from head of $\vec{b}$ to head of $\vec{a}$.
**Scalar multiplication:** $k\vec{a}$ has magnitude $|k|\cdot|\vec{a}|$. If $k>0$, direction unchanged; if $k<0$, direction reversed; if $k=0$, null vector.
Detailed Classification of Vector Types

Equal vectors: Two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction, regardless of their initial points. $\vec{a} = \vec{b} \iff |\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}|$ and direction is identical.
Opposite (negative) vectors: $\vec{b} = -\vec{a}$ means $\vec{b}$ has the same magnitude as $\vec{a}$ but opposite direction.

Unit vector: A vector of magnitude 1. Denoted by a hat: $\hat{a} = \frac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$ for $\vec{a} \neq \vec{0}$. In Cartesian coordinates: $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ are unit vectors along x, y, z axes.
Null (zero) vector: $\vec{0}$ has magnitude 0 and undefined direction. $\vec{a} + \vec{0} = \vec{a}$.
Parallel vectors: $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are parallel if $\vec{a} = k\vec{b}$ for some scalar $k$. They point in the same or opposite direction.
Collinear vectors: Vectors lying on the same line or parallel lines. All parallel vectors are collinear.
Coplanar vectors: Vectors lying in the same plane. Any two vectors are always coplanar; three vectors are coplanar if their scalar triple product is zero.
Position vector: The vector from origin O to point P is $\vec{OP}$. If P has coordinates (x, y, z), then $\vec{OP} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$.
Co-initial vectors: Vectors with the same initial point.
Vector Addition — Detailed Laws

Triangle Law: To add $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, place the tail of $\vec{b}$ at the head of $\vec{a}$. The resultant $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$ is the vector from the tail of $\vec{a}$ to the head of $\vec{b}$.
Parallelogram Law: Place $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ tail-to-tail. Complete the parallelogram. The diagonal from the common tail is $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$.

Component-wise addition: If $\vec{a} = a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = b_1\hat{i} + b_2\hat{j} + b_3\hat{k}$, then $\vec{a} + \vec{b} = (a_1+b_1)\hat{i} + (a_2+b_2)\hat{j} + (a_3+b_3)\hat{k}$.

Properties: Commutative ($\vec{a}+\vec{b}=\vec{b}+\vec{a}$), Associative ($\vec{a}+(\vec{b}+\vec{c})=(\vec{a}+\vec{b})+\vec{c}$), Identity ($\vec{a}+\vec{0}=\vec{a}$), Inverse ($\vec{a}+(-\vec{a})=\vec{0}$).
Vector Subtraction
Subtraction is defined as addition of the negative: $\vec{a} - \vec{b} = \vec{a} + (-\vec{b})$.
Geometric interpretation: Draw $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ from the same point. The vector from the head of $\vec{b}$ to the head of $\vec{a}$ represents $\vec{a} - \vec{b}$.
Component-wise: $\vec{a} - \vec{b} = (a_1-b_1)\hat{i} + (a_2-b_2)\hat{j} + (a_3-b_3)\hat{k}$.
Scalar Multiplication
For scalar $k$ and vector $\vec{a}$: $k\vec{a}$ has magnitude $|k|\cdot|\vec{a}|$.

• $k > 0$: same direction as $\vec{a}$
  • $k < 0$: opposite direction
  • $k = 0$: null vector $\vec{0}$
Properties: $k(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) = k\vec{a} + k\vec{b}$, $(k+m)\vec{a} = k\vec{a} + m\vec{a}$, $(km)\vec{a} = k(m\vec{a})$, $1\vec{a} = \vec{a}$, $(-1)\vec{a} = -\vec{a}$.
Component Form and Direction Cosines
Any vector $\vec{a}$ can be expressed as $\vec{a} = a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}$.
Magnitude: $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}$.

Direction cosines: If $\vec{a}$ makes angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ with x, y, z axes, then $\cos\alpha = \frac{a_1}{|\vec{a}|}$, $\cos\beta = \frac{a_2}{|\vec{a}|}$, $\cos\gamma = \frac{a_3}{|\vec{a}|}$. These satisfy $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$.
Direction ratios: The numbers $a_1, a_2, a_3$ proportional to direction cosines.
Linear Combination and Linear Independence
Linear combination: $\vec{v} = \lambda_1\vec{a}_1 + \lambda_2\vec{a}_2 + \cdots + \lambda_n\vec{a}_n$ for scalars $\lambda_i$.

Linearly independent: Vectors $\vec{a}_1, \vec{a}_2, \dots, \vec{a}_n$ are linearly independent if $\lambda_1\vec{a}_1 + \lambda_2\vec{a}_2 + \cdots + \lambda_n\vec{a}_n = \vec{0} \implies \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \cdots = \lambda_n = 0$.
Linearly dependent: If there exist scalars not all zero such that the linear combination equals $\vec{0}$.
In 3D, maximum 3 vectors can be linearly independent. Any 4 or more vectors are linearly dependent.
Section Formula
If point P divides the line segment joining A($\vec{a}$) and B($\vec{b}$) internally in ratio $m:n$, then $\vec{p} = \frac{m\vec{b} + n\vec{a}}{m+n}$.
External division in ratio $m:n$: $\vec{p} = \frac{m\vec{b} - n\vec{a}}{m-n}$ (for $m \neq n$).
Midpoint: $m=n=1$ gives $\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{2}$.
Collinearity of Points

Three points with position vectors $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$ are collinear if and only if $(\vec{b}-\vec{a})$ and $(\vec{c}-\vec{a})$ are parallel vectors, i.e., $(\vec{b}-\vec{a}) = k(\vec{c}-\vec{a})$ for some scalar $k$.
Equivalently, the vectors are linearly dependent: there exist scalars $x, y, z$ not all zero such that $x\vec{a} + y\vec{b} + z\vec{c} = \vec{0}$ with $x+y+z=0$.
confusion: Do not confuse equal vectors with parallel vectors. Equal vectors must have identical magnitude AND direction. Parallel vectors only need to point in the same or opposite direction (magnitudes can differ).

The zero vector $\vec{0}$ has NO direction. It is not parallel to any specific vector, though some textbooks say it's parallel to all vectors. Be careful with statements like '$\vec{0}$ is parallel to $\vec{a}$' — it's a convention, not a geometric fact.

A unit vector is NOT a vector of length 1 in a specific coordinate direction. $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ are the standard unit vectors, but ANY vector of magnitude 1 is a unit vector (e.g., $(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})$).

The direction cosines $\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma$ are the cosines of the angles with POSITIVE axes. The angles are always between $0$ and $\pi$, so direction cosines can be negative (when the angle is obtuse).
Linear dependence of 3 vectors in 3D means they are COPLANAR (lie in a plane). Linear independence means they span the full 3D space. Do not confuse coplanarity with collinearity (all on one line).

In the section formula, internal division uses $m+n$ in the denominator, while external division uses $m-n$. The formula changes if you swap $m$ and $n$ — be consistent with which point corresponds to which ratio.
practice: Find the unit vector in the direction of $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. Also find a vector of magnitude 5 in the same direction.
If $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$, find $2\vec{a} - 3\vec{b}$ and its magnitude.
Show that the vectors $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$, and $\vec{c} = 3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$ are coplanar.
Find the position vector of the point dividing the line joining A(1, 2, 3) and B(4, 6, 8) internally in the ratio 2:1 and externally in the ratio 2:1.

If $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$, find a vector perpendicular to both $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ using the concept of linear combination (hint: cross product will be covered later, but here use the fact that $(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \cdot \vec{a} = 0$ and $(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \cdot \vec{b} = 0$).

Prove that the points with position vectors $\vec{a} - 2\vec{b} + 3\vec{c}$, $2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b} - 4\vec{c}$, and $-7\vec{b} + 10\vec{c}$ are collinear, where $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$ are non-coplanar vectors.

If $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$ are non-zero non-coplanar vectors, find the value of $\lambda$ for which the vectors $\vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b} + 3\vec{c}$, $-2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b} - 4\vec{c}$, and $\vec{a} - 3\vec{b} + 5\vec{c}$ are coplanar.
universalFacts: Every vector in 3D space can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of three non-coplanar vectors (a basis). The standard basis is $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$.
The triangle inequality for vectors: $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| \le |\vec{a}| + |\vec{b}|$, with equality if and only if $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are parallel and in the same direction.
The section formula is the vector analogue of the weighted average formula in coordinate geometry.
Direction cosines provide the 'direction' part of a vector in a coordinate-free way — they are the components of the unit vector in that direction.
The condition for 3 points to be collinear is equivalent to saying their position vectors are linearly dependent with coefficients summing to zero.
